Changes in the outline of the land are continually taking place on the coasts of the British Isles.
On parts of the east coast of England, such as between Harwich and Walton-on-the-Naze, the sea appears to be slowly encroaching on the land.
Places between Harwich and Walton-on-the-Naze that were grazing-fields twenty or thirty years ago are now covered by the sea at high tide.
At low tide those former grazing-fields are sandy wastes threaded by rivulets of sea-water.
On the south coast of the Isle of Wight, between Sandown and the Culver Cliff, land is also being lost.
The Culver Cliff is the most easterly point of the Isle of Wight.
A fort once stood near the edge of the cliff between Sandown and the Culver Cliff.
It was once possible to climb round the seaward wall of that fort, but it is no longer possible.
The outer sea-wall of the fort slipped into the sea long ago.
Some of the fort's inner fortifications have also slipped into the sea.
The whole fort had to be dismantled so that the inner landward wall would not slip down the cliff along with the ground.
Wind and waves are undermining and honeycombing the cliff.
Wind and waves are weakening the base and body of the cliff, so the upper crust on which the fort was built is slipping away.
If nothing were done to protect it, the cliff would gradually be eaten away and its gravel and clay drawn into the sea.
Left to nature, the Isle of Wight would become a little smaller.
The same loss of land is going on at many places along the coast of the British Isles.
The same loss of land is going on along the coast of Florida and in the Gulf of California.
Heligoland is a small islet in the North Sea.
Heligoland once belonged to Great Britain and was later handed over to Germany.
The sea attacks Heligoland so fiercely that it almost has to be armour-plated to keep it intact.
Heligoland is fenced in stone to protect it from the sea.
Coastal erosion like that on England and Heligoland is happening all over the world.
Coastal erosion has always happened.
Without coastal erosion in past ages there would be no British Isles.
England, Scotland and Ireland were once joined to Europe.
It was once possible to walk across the North Sea from Harwich to the Hook of Holland.
The North Sea was once dry land.
The sea encroached on that land from the north.
The Atlantic Ocean broke through from the south until the English Channel was bored through into the shallow waters of the newly formed North Sea.
Through this process, lands that were once part of Europe became the British Isles.
The sea gives back land as well as taking it away.
Sir Thomas Holditch says that on parts of the Pacific coast of America there is dry land that once lay under the sea, as shown by the shells found on it.
Sir Thomas Holditch says that right next to this raised land a boat can be sailed over forests now sunk beneath the sea.
The loss of parts of England to the sea is a serious matter.
The process by which the sea wears away land is called sea erosion.
A Royal Commission on Sea Erosion was appointed to look into how much land had been lost and how the loss might be remedied.
In some parts of the English coast the land is gaining rather than losing.
The sand, gravel, chalk, shale and clay the sea takes from cliffs are not lost.
Material eroded by the sea makes the sea shallower at the places where tides and currents deposit it.
The sea may lay eroded material down as beds or sand-banks.
The sea may carry eroded material round the coast and drop it somewhere else.
The sea may tear down the coast at one point while building it up at others.
The sea may build natural breakwaters out of material it has taken from elsewhere.
Rivers, like the sea, lay down beds of material.
Every shower of rain washes some sand, gravel, loam or chalk from the land into the nearest rivulet.
Rivulets carry this material to rivers, and rivers carry it to the sea.
A fast-moving river carries most of its sediment along with it.
Rivers are generally muddy after rain.
A river usually slows down as it nears the sea and meets the tides.
When a river slows down it drops its sediment.
Mud-banks or sand-banks form at the mouths of rivers.
If a river is left alone long enough, the sand-banks at its mouth grow until the mouth becomes shallower and spreads.
River mouths silt up over time.
Where a river is used by ships, large sums must be spent dredging mud to keep the channels clear.
Dredging to keep channels clear is done in the Scheldt and at the mouth of the Thames.
